chapters.title: Meet the Pieces
chapters.blurb: How every piece moves, one drill at a time.

lessons.title: The Rook
lessons.explanation: Rooks move in straight lines - any number of squares along a rank (sideways) or a file (up and down). They cannot jump over other pieces, but on an empty board they zoom across.

exercises.instruction: Slide the rook sideways along the first rank: a1 to e1.
exercises.hint: Rooks travel along ranks - straight sideways.

exercises.instruction: Now send the rook up the a-file to a8.
exercises.hint: Files are vertical. a8 also checks the black king!

exercises.instruction: Slide this rook across the first rank to a1.
exercises.hint: Straight sideways, just like before.

lessons.title: The Bishop
lessons.explanation: Bishops slide along diagonals only. Each bishop stays on one colour for its whole life - the c1 bishop will only ever visit dark squares. No straight lines, no jumping over pieces.

exercises.instruction: Slide the bishop along the diagonal to h6.
exercises.hint: c1-d2-e3-f4-g5-h6, one diagonal sweep.

exercises.instruction: Now send it the other way, to a3.
exercises.hint: c1-b2-a3 is the other diagonal.

lessons.title: The Queen
lessons.explanation: The queen is a rook and a bishop combined: straight lines AND diagonals. She is the strongest piece - worth about nine pawns - so keep her safe early on.

exercises.instruction: Push the queen up the d-file to d8.
exercises.hint: Straight line, like a rook.

exercises.instruction: Now glide diagonally to h5.

lessons.title: The Knight
lessons.explanation: Knights move in an L: two squares one way, then one square sideways. They are the only piece that jumps over anything - great for escaping crowded positions.

exercises.instruction: Jump the knight to f3.
exercises.hint: Two up, one left.

exercises.instruction: This time jump to e2.
exercises.hint: Two left, one up.

exercises.instruction: And now to h3.
exercises.hint: Two right... or one right and two up. Your choice of path, same L.

lessons.title: King and Pawns
lessons.explanation: Pawns march forward one square (or two from their starting square) and capture diagonally. They never retreat. The king moves one square in any direction - keep him safe, but he is a fighter in the endgame.

exercises.instruction: Push the pawn two squares: e2 to e4.
exercises.hint: From its starting square a pawn may step two.

exercises.instruction: This time advance it one square to e3.
exercises.hint: Pawns only move forward.

exercises.instruction: Step the king forward to e2.
exercises.hint: One square at a time, any direction.

chapters.title: Check, Escape, Mate
chapters.blurb: Attack the king, dodge attacks, and deliver your first checkmate.

lessons.title: Giving Check
lessons.explanation: A check is an attack on the king. The king must respond immediately: move away, block, or capture the attacker. Let's practice checking.

exercises.instruction: Put the rook on a8 to CHECK the black king.
exercises.hint: The whole a-file is open.

lessons.title: Getting Out of Check
lessons.explanation: When your king is in check you have no time for clever plans - deal with the check first. Here the black rook checks you along the first rank, so step off that rank.

exercises.instruction: Your king is in check! Move him somewhere safe.
exercises.hint: Any square on the second rank is safe. Staying on the first rank is not.

lessons.title: Blocking a Check
lessons.explanation: If the checking piece attacks from far away, you can stop the attack by placing a piece in its path. The bishop checks your king along the diagonal - park the rook in front of the king.

exercises.instruction: Block the bishop's check with your rook.
exercises.hint: The check travels c3-d2-e1. Stand on d2.

lessons.title: Your First Checkmate
lessons.explanation: Checkmate is check with no escape: no safe squares, no block, no capture. Two rooks work beautifully together - one cuts off ranks, the other delivers.

exercises.instruction: Mate in one with the b1 rook!
exercises.hint: The a7 rook already covers the seventh rank. Push the other rook to the eighth.

chapters.title: Winning Material
chapters.blurb: Grab free pieces, and trap defenders with forks.

lessons.title: Hanging Pieces
lessons.explanation: A 'hanging' piece is one that is attacked but not defended. Before every move, scan the board for undefended pieces - they are free gifts.

exercises.instruction: The black queen is completely undefended. Take her!
exercises.hint: Your rook travels straight up the d-file.

lessons.title: The Knight Fork
lessons.explanation: A fork attacks two things at once. Knights are fork specialists - one jump can hit a king and a queen together. The king must move, and then you take the queen.

exercises.instruction: Find the knight move that attacks the queen AND checks the king.
exercises.hint: Look for a square that jumps to both d5 and e8.

lessons.title: Discovered Attack
lessons.explanation: When one piece stands in front of another, moving the front piece 'discovers' the attack of the one behind. Even better: move the front piece WITH a threat, so the opponent has two problems.

exercises.instruction: Move the rook with a check - the bishop behind it will be eyeing the queen.
exercises.hint: Check the black king along the eighth rank.

chapters.title: Endgame Essentials
chapters.blurb: Promote pawns and finish with king and queen.

lessons.title: Promotion
lessons.explanation: When a pawn reaches the last rank it becomes a queen (almost always the best choice). An extra queen usually decides the game on the spot.

exercises.instruction: March the pawn to g8 and promote it.
exercises.hint: One square forward - then choose your new piece (queen!).

lessons.title: Queen and King Mate
lessons.explanation: To mate with king and queen, your king helps by covering escape squares while the queen steps in for the kill - protected by her own king.

exercises.instruction: Mate in one: use your king to protect the queen.
exercises.hint: The queen steps up the g-file, right next to the black king - guarded by yours.

lessons.title: Back-Rank Danger
lessons.explanation: Pawns in front of the king can be a shield or a cage. If the rank behind the pawns is open, a rook or queen can mate instantly. Always give your king breathing room (castling helps!).

exercises.instruction: The black king is caged by its own pawns. Mate in one!
exercises.hint: The a-file leads straight to the eighth rank.

chapters.title: Opening Principles
chapters.blurb: Start every game with the right plan.

lessons.title: Control the Center
lessons.explanation: The four center squares (d4, e4, d5, e5) are the high ground. Pieces in the center see more of the board. Classic first move: king's pawn two squares forward.

exercises.instruction: Grab the center: play e2-e4.
exercises.hint: The king's pawn, two squares forward.

lessons.title: Develop a Knight
lessons.explanation: Bring your pieces off the back rank quickly - knights before bishops is a good rule. The knight to f3 attacks the center and prepares to castle.

exercises.instruction: Black mirrored you. Now develop: knight to f3.
exercises.hint: The classic developing move, attacking e5.

lessons.title: Develop the Bishop
lessons.explanation: Bishops love long open diagonals. The Italian bishop on c4 aims straight at the weakest square in Black's camp: f7.

exercises.instruction: Develop the bishop to c4.
exercises.hint: The Italian Game: Bc4 eyes f7.

lessons.title: Castle Early
lessons.explanation: Castling does two jobs at once: tucks the king behind pawns and brings a rook toward the center. Aim to castle in the first ten moves.

exercises.instruction: Castle kingside: king e1 to g1.
exercises.hint: Tap the king, then the square two to the right. Both f1 and g1 are empty - that is the point!

lessons.title: Fork Recap
lessons.explanation: You met the knight fork in Chapter 3. Here it is again - knights that sit near enemy royalty are always worth a second look.

exercises.instruction: Fork the king and queen with one knight jump.
exercises.hint: Which square attacks both d5 and e8?

lessons.title: Pin Recap
lessons.explanation: A pin freezes a piece: it cannot move without exposing something more valuable behind it. Pinned pieces make perfect targets.

exercises.instruction: The knight is pinned against the king. Win it.
exercises.hint: Your rook on the e-file holds him in place - a pawn can take him.

lessons.title: Pattern: Corner Mate
lessons.explanation: Many beginner games end with a corner mate like this. Memorize the pattern: queen beside the king, protected by her own king.

exercises.instruction: Mate in one with queen and king working together.
exercises.hint: Queen to g7, protected by the king on f6.

lessons.title: Pattern: Promotion Mate
lessons.explanation: Promotion is not just about getting a queen - sometimes the new queen mates instantly. Choose the promoting piece carefully.

exercises.instruction: Promote with checkmate!
exercises.hint: A rook would not cover g7. Pick the right piece.
